content: The EP300 gene encodes the enzyme histone acetyltransferase p300, also referred to as p300 HAT or E1A-associated protein p300. This enzyme plays a pivotal role in regulating gene transcription by modifying chromatin structure through histone acetylation. It is essential for cellular processes such as growth, division, differentiation (the process by which cells mature and acquire specialized functions), and the suppression of tumor formation. The p300 protein is critical for normal development both prenatally and postnatally. The EP300 gene is located on the long arm (q) of chromosome 22 at position 13.2. It is closely related to the CREB-binding protein (CBP) gene, which is located on chromosome 16. The p300 protein functions as a histone acetyltransferase, facilitating transcriptional regulation by remodeling chromatin. It is integral to cellular proliferation and differentiation. Additionally, p300 mediates cAMP-dependent gene regulation by specifically binding to phosphorylated CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein). The protein contains a bromodomain, which is involved in interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling pathways. Furthermore, p300 acts as a co-activator of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1A), thereby contributing to the activation of hypoxia-responsive genes, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). The mechanism of p300 involves its role as a transcriptional co-activator. It achieves this by binding to transcription factors and components of the transcriptional machinery. This interaction is mediated by specific domains within the p300 protein, including the nuclear receptor interaction domain (RID), the KIX domain (which interacts with CREB and MYB), the cysteine/histidine-rich regions (TAZ1/CH1 and TAZ2/CH3), and the interferon response binding domain (IBiD). These domains, particularly KIX, TAZ1, TAZ2, and IBiD, bind tightly to sequences within the transactivation domains (9aaTADs) of transcription factors such as p53. Mutations in the EP300 gene are implicated in Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome, a condition characterized by developmental abnormalities. These mutations typically result in the loss of one functional copy of the gene in each cell, reducing the amount of p300 protein by half. Some mutations produce a truncated, nonfunctional version of the protein, while others completely prevent protein production from one gene copy. Although the precise mechanism by which reduced p300 levels lead to the features of Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome remains unclear, it is evident that the loss of one EP300 gene copy disrupts normal development. Chromosomal rearrangements involving the EP300 gene on chromosome 22 have been associated with certain cancers. For instance, a translocation between chromosomes 8 and 22 has been observed in cases of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Another translocation, involving chromosomes 11 and 22, has been identified in individuals who developed AML following chemotherapy for other cancers. These chromosomal changes disrupt the EP300 gene region, contributing to cancer development. Somatic mutations in EP300, which are acquired during a person’s lifetime and present only in specific cells, have been identified in various cancers, including those of the colon, rectum, stomach, breast, and pancreas. In prostate cancer, EP300 mutations may influence tumor progression and metastasis. These mutations typically result in the loss of functional p300 protein, impairing the cell’s ability to regulate growth and division, thereby promoting tumor formation. The EP300 protein interacts with a wide array of other proteins, including transcription factors, co-activators, and signaling molecules. Some of its known interaction partners include BCL3, BRCA1, CDX2, CEBPB, CITED1, CITED2, DDX5, DTX1, EID1, ELK1, ESR1, FEN1, GPS2, HIF1A, HNF1A, HNRPU, ING4, ING5, IRF2, LEF1, MAF, MAML1, MEF2C, MEF2D, MYBL2, Mdm2, MyoD, MEF2A, NCOA6, NFATC2, NPAS2, P53, PAX6, PCNA, PROX1, PTMA, PPARA, PPARG, RORA, RELA, SMAD1, SMAD2, SMAD7, SNIP1, SS18, STAT3, STAT6, TAL1, TCF3, TFAP2A, TGS1, TRERF1, TSG101, THRA, TWIST1, YY1, and Zif268. These interactions underscore the protein’s extensive involvement in diverse cellular processes and signaling pathways.
